sections.h2: What kind of county is Bureau County for a home seller?
sections.html:
Bureau County is a largely rural county in north-central Illinois, created from Putnam County in 1837 and named for the Bureau brothers, French Canadian traders who ran a post near Big Bureau Creek and the Illinois River. Princeton is both the county seat and the largest city. The county covers 874 square miles, of which 869 are land, and it belongs to the Ottawa micropolitan area. Part of the Hennepin Canal Parkway State Park lies inside it.

With about 38 people per square mile, the market looks different from the suburbs. Many sales involve farmhouses, village homes in places such as Princeton and Tiskilwa, and older houses on larger lots. Winters bring a January low near 14 degrees in Princeton, and the wettest month is August, which is worth remembering when a buyer's inspector looks at a basement or a roof.

  • Census estimate for 2025: 32,510 residents, 2.3% below the 2020 base, with 24.9% aged 65 or older.
  • Housing: 15,663 units, a 76.1% ownership rate and a median owned-home value of $126,900.
  • Rent and income: median gross rent of $832 and median household income of $69,257.
  • Commuting: 21.1 minutes on average, and only 16 building permits were issued in 2025.

sections.h2: Which Bureau County offices do I deal with on property tax?
sections.html:
Two county offices sit in the courthouse at 700 South Main Street in Princeton, and both are open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The treasurer, who doubles as county collector, prepares and collects bills. The Supervisor of Assessments supports the township assessors, processes exemptions, and serves as clerk to the Board of Review.

The township assessor, elected locally, starts the process by finding and valuing property. If a bill reaches you for a house you no longer own, the treasurer asks that it be returned promptly.

sections.h2: How and when do I pay Bureau County property tax?
sections.html:
The county issues a single bill that is payable in two installments, and partial payments are refused. Illinois law treats an installment as late on the later of June 1 or the day after the date printed on the bill (35 ILCS 200/21-15), so the coupon on your own bill is the date to follow. Not getting a bill, or getting it late, does not excuse the tax or the late charge.

  • In the office, only a check or cash is accepted, with checks payable to "Bureau County Collector."
  • By mail to Bureau County Collector, 700 S. Main St., Room 103, Princeton, IL 61356. A postmark on the due date is acceptable.
  • Online by debit or credit card or e-check through Illinois ePAY, which is available only through the second installment due date.
  • If a mortgage company pays your bill, contacting that company is your responsibility.

A canceled check serves as your receipt, and the treasurer will send a separate one if you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

sections.h2: What does a late payment cost in Bureau County?
sections.html:
The treasurer's page sets out three charges. Interest runs at 1.5% per installment per month on payments made after the due date, and the late-payment schedule is printed on the installment coupons. A payment sent without the late fees is returned. A further $10.00 is added to any tax still unpaid after the second installment date, covering publication and the certified delinquent notice.

Once those notices are mailed, the collector takes only certified funds: a cashier's check, money order or cash. Personal and business checks are refused. At the end of each tax year the collector holds a sale of the tax on every parcel still unpaid. A seller who has fallen behind should clear the balance before listing, since an open delinquency will appear in the title search.

sections.h2: How does a Bureau County assessment appeal work?
sections.html:
Illinois assesses nonfarm property at 33 1/3% of fair market value, and the Bureau County Board of Review rules say the same. An owner who disagrees files an appeal form with the Board's clerk, who is the Supervisor of Assessments, no later than 30 days after the assessment list is published for the township. Filing costs nothing, and a separate form is needed for each parcel unless the parcels are contiguous and similarly classified.

The rules focus on market value or equity, and the amount of a tax bill is not a valid complaint. For a home, the Board looks for:

  • Proof of a recent sale or purchase of the property.
  • A recent appraisal from an Illinois certified appraiser, delivered within 30 calendar days after the filing deadline and prepared to professional standards.
  • At least three recent sales of comparable properties, or assessed values of comparables if equity is the issue.
  • Dated photographs when you claim a condition problem.

The Board sends a tentative notice and an unhappy owner has ten days to schedule a hearing. Hearings run in 15-minute slots in the Supervisor of Assessments' office. Owners may speak for themselves or hire an Illinois attorney, and a missed hearing can lead to dismissal. An incomplete form is returned once with ten more calendar days to fix it.

sections.h2: What should I know about exemptions before listing in Bureau County?
sections.html:
The Board of Review rules state that homestead exemptions are applied under state statute and Department of Revenue guidelines, and that the deadline to apply for any of them is December 31. The Supervisor of Assessments processes exemption, preferential assessment and abatement applications and applies them to eligible parcels.

Because exemptions depend on who owns and occupies the home, a buyer should expect to apply in their own name. A seller can ask the Supervisor of Assessments which exemptions are on the parcel today and bring that list to the closing so credits are estimated on real numbers. Bureau County's website has more on the rules and the appeal form, and the county GIS site shows aerial imagery and parcel boundaries.

sections.h2: How are Bureau County taxes handled at closing?
sections.html:
Illinois bills a year behind, so the bill that arrives after a sale usually covers the period before it. The usual approach, described by the Adams and Boone County collectors in their own materials, is a seller credit for the unbilled period, and the same practice is common in Bureau County closings. Ask the title company to order a tax certification from the treasurer's office, which the county can supply at 815-872-3241.

  • Confirm whether both installments for the prior bill are paid.
  • Agree in the contract how the next bill will be split.
  • Give the county the buyer's mailing address, so assessment notices and bills reach the right person.
  • Keep copies of the deed and transfer paperwork, since the Board of Review accepts a recent purchase as evidence of value.

faqs.q: How many installments does Bureau County property tax have?
faqs.a: Two. You receive one bill that is payable in two installments, and the county does not accept partial payments. The coupon on your bill shows each date.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to appeal a Bureau County assessment?
faqs.a: No. The Board of Review rules say there is no fee for filing an appeal. You must file within 30 days after the assessment list is published for your township.

faqs.q: Can I pay Bureau County tax with a credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, online through Illinois ePAY by debit card, credit card or e-check, until the second installment due date. The treasurer's counter accepts only checks and cash.

faqs.q: What happens to Bureau County tax I do not pay?
faqs.a: Interest builds at 1.5% per installment per month, $10.00 is added after the second installment date, and the collector holds a tax sale on unpaid parcels at year end. After notices go out, only certified funds are taken.

faqs.q: Where do I file a homestead exemption in Bureau County?
faqs.a: With the Supervisor of Assessments, 700 South Main Street, Suite 12, Princeton, phone 815-875-6478. The Board of Review rules give December 31 as the deadline to apply.
